overview: Teke communities connected the Congo River’s great markets with forest and savanna producers. The kingdom centred on Mbé and its Makoko formed part of this wider, diverse Teke world. This imported 1878 to 1914 outline covers a period of French colonial intervention, rather than the kingdom’s complete lifespan.

periods.title: Markets and royal authority
periods.summary: Mbé’s court and Congo Pool’s trading communities belonged to a much older regional network.

periods.title: A contested colonial settlement
periods.summary: France used the 1880 documents to claim territory; their meaning and the extent of local consent were disputed.

items.text: The river was a commercial meeting place, not an empty route waiting for Europeans. Teke intermediaries linked communities across forest, marsh and plateau, trading both raw materials and finished goods. Their knowledge of suppliers, customers and routes was an important source of influence.

In 1882 an American diplomat described the French treaty language as difficult to interpret. He also reported Stanley’s claim that a local chief understood his agreement as a land lease. The documents therefore record competing colonial claims as well as African decisions; signing did not create a shared understanding of sovereignty.

Mbé was a capital that moved. According to the royal domain’s heritage record, the capital shifted after a king died, and abandoned royal settlements became sacred forests. Remembering a ruler could therefore mean protecting a living landscape rather than preserving one permanent palace.

The Ngantsibi, or queen, was a guardian of authority during a vacancy in the kingship, rather than simply the king’s wife. Her residence at Ngabé and places of initiation formed part of the royal landscape. Political authority had important female custodians.

Brazza’s 1880 notes describe a royal meal of pounded cassava leaves enriched with pounded kernels, served on plates. He contrasted it with plain leaves eaten in a famine elsewhere. The same staple could become a different meal depending on ingredients, resources and circumstances.

The same visitor watched maize beer being made from grain that was first sprouted and dried, then pounded. Large stores of dried cassava and sprouted maize also appear in his account. Feeding a community involved planning and processing, well before anyone sat down to eat.

On the Congo in September 1880, river travellers declined to cross when wind against the current raised dangerous waves. Experienced paddlers understood when to wait. A canoe journey could have a timetable, but the river still got a vote.

A surviving early twentieth-century Teke raffia cloth is a small square with yellow and black stripes and fringed edges. Woven cloth could carry value as well as pattern: buyers and sellers negotiated its worth through width and quality. A careful weaver was making more than something attractive to wear.

A nineteenth-century ancestor figure preserves a sculptor’s precise slit eyes, patterned cheeks and projecting beard. Its body contains bonga, substances believed to activate ancestral power. Small figures could be sold in markets, while larger works were commissioned for communities: artistic skill supported both households and public life.

French observer Edouard Ponel recorded chiefs using such figures during important discussions in the 1880s. Palm wine and kola became offerings intended to bring ancestors into the conversation. The sculpture was an active participant in decision-making as its users understood it, rather than merely a room decoration.

One Kidumu mask, probably made in the early twentieth century and collected in 1929, divides its design into upper and lower zones. Its performer cartwheeled, connecting the worlds of living people and ancestors through movement. This was one Teke performance tradition, not a uniform custom across every community.

Writing sample: “Au nom de la France” means “In the name of France.” These French words open the act of 3 October 1880 reproduced in the official gazette. They show the language of the colonial claim. They are neither Teke-language writing nor words composed by the Makoko himself.

ending.text: French colonial rule reduced the kingdom’s political independence; 1914 is only this map record’s endpoint. Teke communities and royal traditions continued. The Mbé heritage account records enduring investiture and funeral rites, family genealogies and sacred forests that preserve the memory of earlier rulers.
